title: Stability and dispersion plots: where in wavenumber or in the complex plane does the scheme fail?
summary: Von Neumann and stability-region figures replace a simulation by a function: the factor by which each wavelength is multiplied per step, or the set of values h times lambda a time integrator tolerates. Reading them predicts blow-up before running anything.

read_the_figure.question: For this scheme and CFL number, is any wave amplified, how strongly are short waves damped, and how does the numerical wave speed differ from the true one?
read_the_figure.axes: Amplification-factor figures: x is theta/pi, the phase advance per cell normalised so 0 is a very long wave and 1 is the shortest wave the grid can hold (two cells per wavelength); y is |G|, the factor by which that wave's amplitude is multiplied each step. Stability-region figure: axes are the real and imaginary parts of lambda times dt; blue is where the integrator is stable. Modified-wavenumber figure: x is theta/pi again; y is the imaginary part (phase) or real part (damping) of the numerical wavenumber times dx. CFL sweep: x is CFL number, y the maximum of |phi| at the end of a run.
look_at: |G| = 1 is the neutral line. Any curve above it is a growing wave: the scheme is unstable at that CFL number.
How quickly a curve falls toward the right: it measures how heavily short waves are damped. Zero damping (|G| = 1 everywhere) is the property of centred schemes with implicit time stepping.
Compare the left (CFL 0.4) and right (CFL 0.8) panels: how the curves move with CFL is the stability story.
Overlaid curves hide each other: at CFL 0.4 and 0.8 the purple TVD + FE curve appears to sit on top of the solid blue upwind + FE curve.

Stability regions: locate where the scheme's eigenvalues live. Advection eigenvalues lie on the imaginary axis, diffusion eigenvalues on the negative real axis (the green and blue labels). The integrator must cover that axis out to the value of dt times the largest eigenvalue.
Modified wavenumber: the dashed straight line is exact. The gap below it in the left panel is phase (wave speed) error, which is zero only for very long waves.
read_the_figure.proves: A stability or dispersion plot is an analytic statement about the linear scheme. It proves whether each Fourier mode of the linearised problem grows or decays, and by how much phase error. It does not prove anything about nonlinear behaviour, boundaries or variable coefficients.
if_wrong: |G| above 1 for some theta: unstable, the offending wavelengths grow exponentially (see the CFL sweep right panel).
|G| falling to 0 at theta = pi: the shortest waves are removed in one step; fine for smoothing, fatal for resolving fronts.
A curve missing from the legend or hidden under another: check that every scheme named in the legend is visible.
A phase curve peeling away from the exact line early: the scheme resolves only a few wavelengths per cell count; refine or raise order.
must_check: The CFL number of each panel is stated (0.4 / 0.8 in the amplification figure, 0.5 in the dispersion figure).

Which axis is amplitude and which is phase. The right-hand panel of the dissipation-and-dispersion figure is titled 'phase error proxy' but plots |G| again, the same curves as the left panel, so it carries no phase information.
Whether blown-up runs are drawn: in the CFL-sweep scatter the 'blown up' markers do not appear anywhere in the shaded region.
That the limited (TVD) scheme is nonlinear, so its curve here is one frozen-coefficient reading, not a proof.
Whether the 'LUDS' curve is the standard linear-upwind stencil. See the owner-review note.
as_drawn: Values read from the figures; approximate unless computed below.

Amplification factor: CDS + FE is above 1 everywhere between the ends; its maximum is about 1.08 at CFL 0.4 and about 1.28 at CFL 0.8 (computed: sqrt(1+c^2) = 1.077 and 1.281). CDS + CN lies on |G| = 1.
At theta = pi the plotted upwind-family values are about 0.2 (CFL 0.4) and 0.6 (CFL 0.8), equal to |1 - 2c| (computed).
UDS + RK4 at CFL 0.8 and theta = pi is about 0.27 (computed from the fourth-order polynomial: 0.2704); it rises toward the right end instead of falling.
Dispersion figure (CFL 0.5): CDS + FE peaks near 1.12 (computed: 1.118); UDS + CN reaches 1/3 at theta = pi (computed); TVD + FE reaches 0.

Stability regions: forward Euler is a disc of radius 1 centred at -1; RK2 reaches about 1.7 up the imaginary direction; RK4 reaches about 2.8 on the imaginary axis; backward Euler and Crank-Nicolson cover the whole left half plane (Crank-Nicolson's boundary is the imaginary axis).
CFL sweep (UDS + FE): drawn points are all stable up to CFL = 1 with max |phi| at t = 2 between about 0.55 and 1.0; at CFL 1.1 the profile oscillates between the plot clip limits of plus and minus 5.

terms.meaning: A single sine-cosine wave exp(i k x). A linear constant-coefficient scheme treats each mode independently.
The complex number G by which a mode is multiplied in one time step. |G| is the change of amplitude; arg G is the change of phase.
The advance of a wave across one cell: theta = k dx. It runs from 0 to pi on a grid.
The numerical domain of dependence must contain the physical one; for explicit upwind it limits c to 1.
The set of complex z = lambda dt for which a time integrator applied to y' = lambda y does not grow.
An integrator whose stability region contains the entire left half plane (backward Euler, Crank-Nicolson).
The wavenumber a discrete derivative actually represents: its imaginary part is the phase, its real part the damping.
Dissipation changes amplitude (|G| below 1); dispersion changes speed per wavelength (phase error).

remember: Stable means |G| <= 1 for every theta. One bad wavelength is enough.
Upwind with forward Euler is stable exactly for 0 <= c <= 1.
Central differencing with forward Euler is unstable for every c.
Explicit integrators have bounded stability regions; A-stable ones (backward Euler, Crank-Nicolson) do not, but A-stability is not accuracy.
Short waves are the ones that suffer: phase error and damping both grow toward theta = pi.

understand.title: From a simulation to a function
understand.text: Put exp(i k x) into the scheme. Because the scheme is linear and the grid uniform, the mode keeps its shape and is only multiplied by G each step. Stability then becomes a statement about a single complex function on [0, pi].

understand.title: Why |G| above 1 means blow-up
understand.text: After N steps the amplitude is |G|^N. A factor only slightly above one, for example 1.08, compounds: 1.08 raised to 100 is about 2200. The figure's tiny red bump is not small in practice.

understand.title: Two ways of looking at the same fact
understand.text: A time integrator is stable if dt times each eigenvalue of the spatial operator falls in its region. Von Neumann analysis with the full scheme is the same statement; the region plot separates the time integrator from the spatial scheme, so you can mix them.

understand.title: What the eigenvalues look like
understand.text: Centred advection: purely imaginary. Diffusion: negative real. Upwind advection: a circle in the left half plane. Match them to the region: forward Euler barely touches the imaginary axis, so it cannot handle centred advection; RK4 covers a stretch of it.

understand.title: Phase error is invisible to |G|
understand.text: A scheme can have |G| = 1 (no damping) and still be wrong: a wave that travels at the wrong speed ends in the wrong place. Phase has to be read from the modified wavenumber or from arg G.

steps.title: Insert a Fourier mode
steps.note: The same trick as separation of variables on a grid. Each mode evolves independently.

steps.title: Upwind with forward Euler
steps.note: Expand the modulus squared. The second term is negative for 0 < c < 1, so |G| < 1; for c > 1 it is positive and long waves already grow.

steps.title: The CFL limit follows
steps.note: This is the CFL bound that the sweep figure shows: stable points up to CFL 1, blow-up above it.

steps.title: Central differencing with forward Euler
steps.note: The derivative of the exponential is purely imaginary, so G sits above the real axis by c sin(theta). Its modulus is above one for every c, with the maximum sqrt(1+c^2) at theta = pi/2, as plotted.

steps.title: Crank-Nicolson removes the growth
steps.note: A number divided by its own complex conjugate has modulus one. Neutral stability, hence the flat dashed line in the amplification figure; the price is a phase error.

steps.title: Stability region of forward Euler
steps.note: For y' = lambda y the update is y times (1 + z). The set where this does not grow is a disc of radius one centred at -1, the first panel of the stability-region figure.

steps.title: Stability region of an implicit integrator
steps.note: For backward Euler the region is the outside of the disc centred at +1, which contains the whole left half plane.

steps.title: Modified wavenumber of upwind and central schemes
steps.note: The real part is damping (1 - cos theta, up to 2), the imaginary part is the phase (sin theta instead of theta). This is why the two schemes share one curve in the left panel and only upwind appears in the right panel.

analyze.q: In the amplification figure the TVD + FE curve appears to coincide with solid-blue UDS + FE. Is that plausible? What does it say about the limiter in a frozen-coefficient analysis?
analyze.hint: Where a limiter switches to the upwind flux the two schemes have the same stencil.

analyze.q: The right-hand panel of the dissipation-and-dispersion figure repeats the left-hand curves. What information is missing there, and how would you compute it from G?
analyze.hint: Phase error is the argument of G compared with the exact phase, -c theta.

analyze.q: RK4 stability reaches about 2.8 on the imaginary axis. What is the largest CFL number for central advection with RK4?
analyze.hint: The largest imaginary eigenvalue of central advection is a/dx.

evaluate.q: Crank-Nicolson with central differencing is neutrally stable for any CFL number. Is it therefore the best choice for advection? Use the modified-wavenumber figure.
evaluate.hint: Stability is not accuracy: short waves still have the wrong speed.

create: Draw the stability-region diagram for the integrator you use most, mark where your problem's eigenvalues land at your time step, and state the margin.
Design a figure that puts amplitude and phase error of one scheme in one panel (a polar plot of G is one option) so the right-hand 'proxy' panel is no longer needed.

checks.answer: After N steps a mode has amplitude |G|^N. Below one it decays, above one it grows without bound, so one is the neutral boundary.

checks.q: What is |G| at theta = pi for upwind with forward Euler at CFL 0.4?
checks.answer: |1 - 0.8| = 0.2, matching the end of the purple and blue solid curves in the left panel.

checks.q: Why does explicit central differencing blow up even at tiny CFL?
checks.hint: Where do its eigenvalues lie and what does the forward-Euler region look like there?
checks.answer: Its eigenvalues are purely imaginary, and the forward Euler region touches the imaginary axis only at the origin, so any dt gives |G| = sqrt(1 + c^2 sin^2 theta) > 1. Smaller c only slows the growth.

checks.q: A colleague says the scheme is fine because the CFL sweep shows no blown-up markers. What do you check?
checks.hint: The right panel and the legend.

checks.q: How would you produce a modified-wavenumber plot for a new stencil?
checks.hint: Apply the stencil to exp(i j theta).
checks.answer: Apply the stencil to the mode exp(i j theta), divide by the mode and by dx, and solve for k star: the imaginary part is the phase and the real part the damping. Plot both against theta/pi with the exact line k = theta as reference.
